genZNote: One of the first bacteria to colonize a newborn's mouth — mostly just here to keep the peace.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human oral cavity and upper respiratory tract mucosa (tongue, saliva)
habitat.hostAssociation: An early and abundant colonizer of the infant oral cavity; a core member of normal oral/salivary flora throughout life

culture.growthCharacteristics: Facultative anaerobe; grows better with added CO2
culture.hemolysis: Alpha-hemolytic or non-hemolytic (viridans group), variable by strain

biochemicalTests.result: Resistant (distinguishes viridans strep from S. pneumoniae)

identificationClues: Gram-positive coccus in chains, catalase negative
Alpha-hemolytic or non-hemolytic on blood agar — part of the viridans streptococcus group
Optochin resistant and bile-insoluble, distinguishing it from Streptococcus pneumoniae

diseases: Rare bacteremia/infective endocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised or post-dental-procedure patients
Rare cases of meningitis after spinal/epidural anesthesia (breach of aseptic technique)
virulenceFactors: Low intrinsic virulence; some strains produce bacteriocins (salivaricins) that inhibit competing oral bacteria
clinicalImportance.transmission: Transmitted via saliva; established in the oral cavity from early infancy
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most abundant organisms of the normal oral microbiome; some strains are studied/marketed as oral probiotics for their bacteriocin production
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Rarely of diagnostic significance; recovered incidentally in oral/respiratory cultures as normal flora

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Catalase negative; generally non-hemolytic to alpha-hemolytic
examFacts.importantTest: Optochin resistance and bile insolubility distinguish viridans strep from S. pneumoniae
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A dominant, generally harmless member of the normal oral microbiome; some strains produce bacteriocins that suppress competing bacteria
